paper.title: Believe it or not: Designing a Human-AI Partnership for Mixed-Initiative Fact-Checking
paper.abstract: Fact-checking, the task of assessing the veracity of claims, is an important, timely, and challenging problem. While many automated fact-checking systems have been recently proposed, the human side of the partnership has been largely neglected: how might people understand, interact with, and establish trust with an AI fact-checking system? Does such a system actually help people better assess the factuality of claims? In this paper, we present the design and evaluation of a mixed-initiative approach to fact-checking, blending human knowledge and experience with the efficiency and scalability of automated information retrieval and ML. In a user study in which participants used our system to aid their own assessment of claims, our results suggest that individuals tend to trust the system: participant accuracy assessing claims improved when exposed to correct model predictions. However, this trust perhaps goes too far: when the model was wrong, exposure to its predictions often degraded human accuracy. Participants given the option to interact with these incorrect predictions were often able improve their own performance. This suggests that transparent models are key to facilitating effective human interaction with fallible AI models.
paper.notes: The system follows an information-literacy-inspired sequence of retrieving relevant articles, assessing article stance and source reputation, and aggregating this evidence into a claim-veracity prediction.

system.name: Mixed-Initiative Fact-Checking System
system.description: A mixed-initiative fact-checking interface that retrieves evidence for a claim, predicts article stances and source reputations, and aggregates them into a claim-veracity prediction. Users can inspect supporting evidence and override stance or reputation estimates to immediately update the overall prediction.
system.processScope: From a user-provided claim through automated evidence retrieval and prediction to evidence inspection and slider-based correction of model estimates.
system.notes: The paper does not assign a separate product name to the prototype. Article stance and source reputation overrides are independently repeatable, and each slider change immediately recomputes the overall claim-veracity prediction. The article-retrieval implementation is not described in enough detail to decompose further.

paper.title: Sensecape: Enabling Multilevel Exploration and Sensemaking with Large Language Models
paper.abstract: People are increasingly turning to large language models (LLMs) for complex information tasks like academic research or planning a move to another city. However, while they often require working in a nonlinear manner — e.g., to arrange information spatially to organize and make sense of it, current interfaces for interacting with LLMs are generally linear to support conversational interaction. To address this limitation and explore how we can support LLM-powered exploration and sensemaking, we developed Sensecape, an interactive system designed to support complex information tasks with an LLM by enabling users to (1) manage the complexity of information through multilevel abstraction and (2) switch seamlessly between foraging and sensemaking. Our within-subject user study reveals that Sensecape empowers users to explore more topics and structure their knowledge hierarchically, thanks to the externalization of levels of abstraction. We contribute implications for LLM-based workflows and interfaces for information tasks.

system.name: Sensecape
system.description: An LLM-powered information exploration and sensemaking environment combining a spatial canvas with a hierarchical organization of topic-specific canvases. Users explore topics through generated responses, questions, explanations, and subtopics, while organizing information through direct manipulation, semantic zoom, and navigation across abstraction levels.
system.processScope: Core interaction processes in the canvas and hierarchy views, including LLM-assisted exploration, text extraction, semantic zoom, semantic dive, and hierarchical organization.
system.notes: Sensecape supports nonlinear, iterative exploration rather than a fixed end-to-end sequence. Processes represent distinct interaction modes described in Section 3.2 and Figures 3–7. Users can repeatedly invoke exploration actions on existing or generated nodes, reorganize information, and move between abstraction levels. LLM generation and summarization are stochastic, whereas direct manipulation and view navigation are treated as deterministic interface operations. Semantic zoom involves LLM-generated alternative representations followed by deterministic selection according to zoom level or manual settings. The paper does not specify that semantic zoom summaries are regenerated on every zoom interaction. The current implementation does not include automatic context-aware suggestions for grouping existing nodes or restructuring the hierarchy.

paper.title: Improving Steering and Verification in AI-Assisted Data Analysis with Interactive Task Decomposition
paper.abstract: LLM-powered tools like ChatGPT Data Analysis, have the potential to help users tackle the challenging task of data analysis programming, which requires expertise in data processing, programming, and statistics. However, our formative study (n=15) uncovered serious challenges in verifying AI-generated results and steering the AI (i.e., guiding the AI system to produce the desired output). We developed two contrasting approaches to address these challenges. The first (Stepwise) decomposes the problem into step-by-step subgoals with pairs of editable assumptions and code until task completion, while the second (Phasewise) decomposes the entire problem into three editable, logical phases: structured input/output assumptions, execution plan, and code. A controlled, within-subjects experiment (n=18) compared these systems against a conversational baseline. Users reported significantly greater control with the Stepwise and Phasewise systems, and found intervention, correction, and verification easier, compared to the baseline. The results suggest design guidelines and trade-offs for AI-assisted data analysis tools.

system.name: Interactive Task Decomposition
system.description: An AI-assisted data analysis system that enables users to steer and verify LLM-generated analysis by editing assumptions, execution plans, and code. It implements two decomposition approaches, Phasewise and Stepwise, alongside a conversational baseline.
system.processScope: Dataset and task specification, AI-generated task decomposition, human intervention, code generation and execution, verification, and iterative refinement across three interface variants.
system.notes: Phasewise decomposes the entire task into editable assumptions, an execution plan, and code. Stepwise incrementally generates subgoals, each containing editable assumptions and corresponding code. The Conversational baseline generates non-editable assumptions and code for the entire task, with refinement through follow-up prompts. In Phasewise and Stepwise, submitting an edit to an earlier component regenerates downstream components and preserves the original in a separate branch. Edits to the final component do not create a new branch. Shared side conversations allow code questions, code generation, and exploratory data queries without changing the main analysis. The processes below represent these distinct interaction modes and one iteration of recurring interactions.

paper.title: DiscipLink: Unfolding Interdisciplinary Information Seeking Process via Human-AI Co-Exploration

system.name: DiscipLink
system.description: An interactive human-AI co-exploration system that generates discipline-specific exploratory questions from research interests, expands selected questions into literature search queries, and organizes retrieved papers into contextualized themes. Users can refine exploration directions, inspect and collect papers, and initiate new searches from discovered literature.
system.processScope: Orientation through exploratory question generation, literature retrieval through query expansion, contextualized clustering and paper screening, and bottom-up exploration through paper collections and citation networks.
system.notes: The system uses GPT-4 for generative operations, Semantic Scholar for paper retrieval, text-embedding-3-small for embeddings, and DBSCAN for clustering. Processes represent distinct interaction modes and computational pipelines rather than a mandatory linear sequence. Users may return to orientation from discovered papers and repeat literature searches with new or modified exploratory questions.

paper.title: ImaginationVellum: Generative-AI Ideation Canvas with Spatial Prompts, Generative Strokes, and Ideation History

paper.title: GenTune: Toward Traceable Prompts to Improve Controllability of Image Refinement in Environment Design

system.name: GenTune
system.description: A human-AI image generation and refinement system that connects visual elements to labels extracted from structured prompts. Users can select image elements and refine them through natural-language instructions or reference images using controlled-seed prompt regeneration or semantic-guided inpainting.
system.processScope: Initial image generation, prompt-element correspondence, global refinement, semantic-guided prompt refinement, semantic-guided inpainting, and contextual refinement suggestions.
system.notes: The system uses separate LLM modules for brainstorming, label extraction, refinement, inpainting, and suggestions. SAM segments user-selected image regions, while CLIP matches these regions against labels extracted from the structured prompt. Refinement produces four image candidates per iteration: four controlled-seed results, four inpainting results, or two of each in mixed mode. Users select a candidate to continue refining. The refinement processes describe one iteration and can recur using the selected image and its associated prompt. Controlled-seed regeneration can overwrite previous inpainting modifications. Reference-image captioning is optional, and suggestion generation is independent of executing a refinement.
